tuning approaches. Speciﬁcally, we train GPT-3, an autoregressive language model with 175 billion

cloze tasks, as well as several tasks that require on-the-ﬂy reasoning or domain adaptation, such as
unscrambling words, using a novel word in a sentence, or performing 3-digit arithmetic. At the same
time, we also identify some datasets where GPT-3’s few-shot learning still struggles, as well as some
datasets where GPT-3 faces methodological issues related to training on large web corpora. Finally,

There has also been work on improving the general few-shot prompting abilities of language models (Gao
et al., 2021; Schick & Schütze, 2021, inter alia). Theoretical and interpretability research (Wei et al., 2021a;
Saunshi et al., 2021) on why a language modeling objective facilitates certain downstream behavior could in

available to the community more broadly (Bommasani et al., 2021; Ganguli et al., 2022; Liang et al., 2022).

I have strong coverage. The corpus search across all 100 PDFs shows the answer is anchored in one document — the GPT-3 paper (2005.14165, "Language models are few-shot learners"), which has 20 matching pages — with supporting framing in the emergent-abilities survey (2206.07682) and a distinct methodological use in the Vision Transformer paper (2010.11929). The remaining hits are bibliography citations to the GPT-3 paper rather than substantive discussion. The excerpts are detailed enough to answer directly.

## Few-shot learning

**Definition and the core idea.** The canonical treatment in this corpus is Brown et al., *"Language models are few-shot learners"* (GPT-3). They define few-shot learning as **in-context learning**: the model is given a natural-language task description plus "as many demonstrations as will fit into the model's context window (typically 10 to 100)," then asked to complete a new example — all at inference time, **"without any gradient updates or fine-tuning"** (2005.14165, p. 5; p. 1). It sits on a spectrum with **one-shot** (exactly one demonstration) and **zero-shot** (only an instruction, no demonstrations), all three contrasted with traditional fine-tuning, which instead updates weights on "thousands or tens of thousands of examples" (2005.14165, p. 1, p. 7 / Figure 2.1).

**How it's operationalized.** For each evaluation example, K examples are drawn at random from that task's training set and concatenated as conditioning context (delimited by newlines) ahead of the query; the model then produces the answer in a single forward pass (2005.14165, p. 10). Figure 2.1 summarizes the four regimes and notes GPT-3 is "typically presented with a few dozen examples in the few-shot setting" (2005.14165, p. 7).

**Why it matters / the headline result.** The paper's thesis is that **scaling** the model (GPT-3 = 175B parameters) makes task-agnostic few-shot performance strong enough to sometimes rival prior fine-tuned state-of-the-art across translation, QA, cloze, and on-the-fly reasoning tasks (e.g., word unscrambling, using a novel word, 3-digit arithmetic) — with no fine-tuning datasets required (2005.14165, p. 1). Gains from few-shot learning **grow with model size**: on adversarial Winogrande, scaling is smooth and few-shot GPT-3 175B is competitive with a fine-tuned RoBERTa-large (2005.14165, p. 16, Figure 3.5). Few-shot framing also solves task-specific quirks — e.g., on LAMBADA it lets the model infer that a single-word cloze completion is wanted, replacing older stop-word filtering hacks (2005.14165, p. 12). The paper is candid about limits: it identifies datasets where few-shot GPT-3 "still struggles" (2005.14165, p. 1).

**Broader framing — few-shot prompting as an emergent ability.** Wei et al.'s emergent-abilities survey re-casts this as **few-shot prompting**: a pre-trained model is given a few input–output examples as a preamble and performs an unseen task "without any further training or gradient updates," crediting Brown et al. (2020) as the origin (2206.07682, p. 3). It argues emergent few-shot ability can be influenced by more than raw scale — certain pre-training data features (long-range coherence, many rare classes) and even specific model architectures can enable or require it (2206.07682, p. 8).

**A different, non-LLM sense of the term.** In the Vision Transformer paper, "few-shot" appears as an **evaluation protocol**, not a prompting method: to save compute they report *"few-shot linear accuracy"* — fitting a cheap linear probe on a small labeled subset of frozen features — instead of full fine-tuning, when comparing ViT vs. ResNet across dataset-size subsets (2010.11929, p. 7). This is the metric-learning/linear-probe usage of "few-shot," distinct from GPT-3's in-context demonstrations.

---

**Note on the rest of the corpus:** across all 100 PDFs, other appearances of the phrase are bibliographic references to the GPT-3 paper (e.g., 2010.14701 p. 36; 2205.14135 p. 11; 2605.06546 p. 11 — the latter citing *Flamingo: a visual language model for few-shot learning*) or passing mentions of few-shot learning as future work (1712.00409 p. 12), rather than substantive treatments. The substantive answer is carried by 2005.14165, with framing from 2206.07682 and the separate evaluation-protocol sense from 2010.11929.
